extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of humorous character sketches (Victorian satire / Dickens readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and render comic social types by exaggerating a single dominant trait (friendliness, militarism, politics, domesticity, censoriousness, or buffoonery) and illustrating it with concrete actions, mannerisms, and situational examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Friendly Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerate an obsessive, universal friendliness so that the character makes every person and situation about their own affability (e.g., Mr. Mincin’s extreme friendliness made it impossible to talk about anything in which he had not the chief concern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show friendliness through concrete, comic actions: incessant compliments (to others and himself), dramatic toasts, over-attentive behaviour at parties (balancing attention among guests, carrying women to supper, leading nervous singers out and reviving them with wine), and repeated anecdotal recollections that centre the friend. Use reputation effects (mothers call him an oracle, daughters a dear) and small absurdities (saving acquaintances’ lives fourteen times) to heighten the satire. The humor comes from the relentless, self-important generosity and how it dominates social interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Military Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Base the comic type on an enthusiastic, superficial devotion to military trappings and manner rather than to actual soldiery or courage (obsession with uniforms, lace, bands, epaulettes; swaggering conduct; theatrical posturing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide the type into (a) civilians who worship military life and (b) real young officers who affect grand carriage. Use obsessive, technical detail about uniforms and trappings (buttons, gold lace, stripes) to comic effect. Stage set-pieces: long, reverent contemplation of sentries or Horse Guards; swaggering promenades with clanking heels and sword-carrying that suggest ferocity but are actually performative; theatrical behaviour at the theatre (keeping a 'sharp look-out' to assure audience of defence). Contrast genuine veteran officers’ dignity with the young pretenders’ bluster. The device: show pompous display divorced from real danger or substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Political Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray a person whose whole mental vision is coloured by party politics; everything is read through 'political glasses' and becomes an opportunity for declamation, aphorism, or partisan sneer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize through obsessional topics (the constitution, the people, church and state, Ireland, the Pope) and by using stock phrases and short aphorisms as rhetorical badges. Show two variants—Conservative (vague dogmas, proud declamations) and Radical/Utilitarian (theoretical questions, parliamentary aphorisms, policy pedantry). Use social scenes where the political young gentleman forces political reading on inappropriate settings (dinner-tables, assemblies), hunts for any political allusion, and alienates non-political company (especially ladies). The satirical advice: these talkers should be discountenanced; their persistence is comic because it is socially misplaced and one-note.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Domestic Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch a mild, homebound young man whose life and conversation revolve around his mother and domestic minutiae (Felix Nixon: near-sighted, prim, tremulous voice, Indiarubber goloshes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build humor from minute, exaggerated domestic detail and melodramatic anecdotes (mother’s bulletins of health, timid rage at a coachman, stories of reading late at night requiring doctors and 'blue pills'). Show his primness through possessions (books and flute with peculiar shelves), small ceremonials (holding a skein while a girl winds silk), and harmless gallantry (escorting a young lady five doors off in slippers and goloshes). Emphasize inoffensiveness and genteel self-importance: he is set down as a 'thorough old bachelor' whose peculiarities harm nobody. The comic effect is affectionate ridicule of suburban domesticity and over-attention to trivial personal narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Censorious Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a character who maintains an air of superior judgment through sarcasm, dubious sneers, equivocal smiles, and intentionally ambiguous remarks that make others infer depth and severity (Mr. Fairfax’s mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the censorious type by giving him mannerisms: half-smiles, enigmatic 'ay, ay' replies, repeating words when at a loss, pursing lips, nodding sagely. Let him use minimal content to imply great meaning so that others over-interpret him. Make him the supposed critic of plays, music, and people—always sounding severe but saying little substantive—thereby building a reputation among acquaintances. Show social dynamics: women's curiosity and speculation about his inner life; the censorious man enjoys, and cultivates, the mystery. The satire targets pretentious negativity and performative cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Funny Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict a comic performer whose presence and physical antics induce uproarious laughter (Mr. Griggins: imitative contortions, pantomime, puns, self-styled clowning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey funniness through timing and physicality: a startling knock that causes screams, a theatrical entrance, pantomimic contortions imitating clowns, and a string of puns and jests. Show audience reaction (roars of laughter, clapping, children’s delight, some guests overwhelmed) to establish his reputation as a 'wit of the first water.' Use small excesses (squeezing into laps, likening himself to 'love among the roses') and comic stage business to demonstrate how the funny young gentleman monopolizes mirth. The device: a performer self-aware of his role who uses mimicry and convivial buffoonery to unite and exhaust his audience.
